title: K-beauty stocks rally as Korean brands top Amazon bestseller lists globally ahead of Black Friday
description: People walk past a Black Friday Week Amazon advertisement in Warsaw, Poland, on November 21, 2025. (Photo by Aleksander Kalka/NurPhoto via Getty Image
body: People walk past a Black Friday Week Amazon advertisement in Warsaw, Poland, on November 21, 2025. (Photo by Aleksander Kalka/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesSouth Korean beauty stocks jumped Thursday as the country's skincare brands dominated Amazon's bestseller rankings ahead of Black Friday. Shares of K-beauty giant APR climbed 3.77%, while cosmetic contracts manufacturers Kolmar Korea and Cosmax gained 5.46% and 2.91%, respectively.APR shares, in particular, have rallied sharply this week, up 28%, defying a broader market sell-off in Seoul markets, with the benchmark Kospi index down 2.65% during the same period.A cosmetic sector index tracked by Meritz Securities had gained 12% this week until Wednesday, according to a Thursday note from the brokerage. The rally reflects renewed optimism over earnings growth following strong performances by K-beauty brands across major e-commerce platforms in the U.S. and Europe with Black Friday sales already underway, as well as increasingly attractive valuations following months of share price declines, according to Meritz.K-beauty products topped Amazon's skincare bestseller rankings across six major markets — the U.S., the U.K., Germany, France, Spain and Italy — as of Nov. 25, according to data compiled by Meritz Securities. Other Korean beauty brands, including Biodance, Illiyoon and Anua, also ranked among the top 10 in the U.S., the data showed. As of Thursday morning, Korean beauty products occupied several of the top spots in Amazon's U.S. beauty and personal care category, the e-commerce website showed.Meritz Securities expects APR shares to maintain their positive momentum through the year-end, with a more substantial rebound in early 2027.The brokerage named APR and Cosmax as its top picks in the cosmetics sector. Korean beauty brands have established an "overwhelming presence" in the bestseller rankings of major e-commerce platforms during Black Friday sales, prompting the market to reassess the growth's potential, the brokerage said.

schema.headline: K-beauty stocks rally as Korean brands top Amazon bestseller lists globally ahead of Black Friday

title: South Korea's Kospi leads gains as tech rebound lifts Asia markets
description: An electronic stock board inside the Kabuto One building in Tokyo, Japan, on Tuesday, Jan. 28, 2025. Toru Hanai | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAsia-Pacific
body: An electronic stock board inside the Kabuto One building in Tokyo, Japan, on Tuesday, Jan. 28, 2025. Toru Hanai | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAsia-Pacific markets rose Thursday, tracking Wall Street gains overnight, with tech stocks rebounding from steep losses in the prior session.Investors appear to have looked past a fresh set of U.S. tariffs unveiled by the White House on Wednesday, targeting more than a dozen major trading partners, including China and the European Union.South Korea's Kospi gained 1.73%, while the small-cap Kosdaq index advanced 2.32% after the country's central bank hiked benchmark lending rates by an expected 25 basis points, as inflation continues to run above target while a booming economy allows it room to tighten policy.The central bank raised rates to 3.25%, a 2-year high, in its final meeting of the year, data on the Bank of Korea's website showed.Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 1.21% while the Topix edged 0.71% higher. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was up 0.15%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index rose 1.46% while mainland China's CSI 300 added 0.12%.Asian technology stocks rebounded sharply Thursday, led by Japanese chip-related companies. SoftBank Group surged more than 11%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest rose 7.3%. Lasertec and Disco both gained more than 6%, while Tokyo Electron climbed 4.6%. In South Korea, memory chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics advanced more than 4% and 2.1%, respectively. The gains followed a bruising session Wednesday amid renewed concerns over the sustainability of artificial intelligence spending.Cryptocurrencies also traded higher, with bitcoin rising 1.58% to $60,944.60, while ether gained 1.15% to $1,702.96. The gains come amid lingering concerns over the outlook for digital assets, with the co-founder of now-shuttered crypto exchange BitMEX Arthur Hayes telling CNBC on Tuesday that bitcoin could test $50,000 if the Nasdaq continues to slide.Meanwhile, fresh U.S. inflation data reinforced expectations of further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% year on year in October, accelerating from 3.7% in September, while core inflation came in slightly above expectations at 3.3%.Overnight in the U.S., the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased an 1,100-point plunge on Wednesday, advancing 164.25 points, or 0.33%, to end at 50,182.95. The Nasdaq Composite, however, fell 0.62% to 23,585.80, while the S&P 500 shed 0.25% to close at 7,182.78.U.S. markets will be closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and will have a shortened trading session on Friday.

schema.headline: South Korea's Kospi leads gains as tech rebound lifts Asia markets

title: Liesman: Why Greenspan could bet on productivity — and Warsh needs to hike
description: watch nowIn a discussion on CNBC's Halftime Report Wednesday, the question came up: Why can't Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh hold the line on in
body: watch nowIn a discussion on CNBC's Halftime Report Wednesday, the question came up: Why can't Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh hold the line on interest rates the way his icon Alan Greenspan did at the beginning of the dot-com era?Greenspan famously leaned against inflation hawks on his committee in 1995 and 1996, holding the line on interest rates amid strong growth, because he believed in the productivity promise of the internet revolution.It would be nice if Warsh could follow the same playbook amid the artificial intelligence build-out and keep rates steady until the productivity arrives. Unfortunately, a quick look at the numbers shows just how different the situation is for Warsh when it comes to inflation, the magnitude of the capital-investment boom and the monetary and fiscal stimulus boosting the economy.Former Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan, and current Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh.Consolidated News Pictures | Archive Photos | Getty ImagesBottom line: the Fed looks like it has to hike — and maybe substantially — to be anywhere close to the position where the Fed was in Greenspan's time at the dawn of a major technological revolution.Here are some key points:The nominal Fed funds rate was substantially higher in 1995 than it is today. The real, or inflation adjusted, funds rate was a positive 3.75% back then, and it's now at zero. So the Fed was leaning against the dotcom boom. Greenspan just decided not to lean more. Today, at a zero real rate, the Fed could be said to be fueling the boom.Inflation, as measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index, was substantially lower, right about target at 1.99% (even though there wasn't a formal 2% target then). It's above target now, at 3.8% according to government data published today, and going the wrong way.The current investment boom now is absolutely off the charts compared with the dot-com era. No real comparison. In 1995, spending on information processing equipment rose 15% year over year. In 2025, it was 27%. Looking at the latest data reported today, it grew 60% in the third quarter at an annualized rate. In the second quarter of 1995, it was 18%. Government deficit spending is substantially more stimulative now than it was then. In 1995, the deficit was just 2.2% of GDP. Today, it's 6.2%. Add higher oil prices, higher tariffs and the recent tax cuts and accelerated depreciation on investments, and there's a lot for the Fed to lean against. It may be that the massive capex spending on AI will mean more productivity and less inflation down the road. But the front-end build-out is proving to be more inflationary, and more challenging, to a Fed already dealing with high inflation. In many ways, that's the opposite of what Greenspan had to handle.

schema.headline: Liesman: Why Greenspan could bet on productivity — and Warsh needs to hike

title: Hedge funds are no longer just for the rich. They’re wooing everyday investors
description: The New York Stock Exchange in New York on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesFor decades, hedge funds were the preserve of
body: The New York Stock Exchange in New York on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesFor decades, hedge funds were the preserve of billionaires, pension funds and deep-pocketed institutional investors. Now, the industry is increasingly courting a new pool of capital: everyday investors.The shift, dubbed by some as the "retailization" of hedge funds, comes as alternative asset managers seek new avenues for growth and investors look for ways to shield their portfolios from increasingly volatile equity markets.Unlike traditional equity funds, which typically rely on stocks rising to generate returns, hedge funds can employ strategies including short selling, arbitrage and derivatives to seek profits across different market conditions.Hedge funds are entrepreneurs. Their objective is to make as much money as they possibly can, both in returns and for their organization.Don SteinbruggeAgecroft PartnersFor an industry already managing record levels of assets, individual investors represent a largely untapped growth opportunity, experts who spoke to CNBC said."Hedge funds are entrepreneurs. Their objective is to make as much money as they possibly can, both in returns and for their organization," said Don Steinbrugge, CEO of hedge fund consulting firm Agecroft Partners."So if they have the ability to go after a new market and grow their business, they're going to do that."The push is coming from both hedge fund managers seeking to broaden their investor base and traditional asset managers looking to capitalize on growing demand for alternative investments, said Ken Heinz, president of hedge fund research firm HFR."Heightened geopolitical uncertainty, greater market volatility, inflation concerns, and the higher correlation between equities and bonds have raised questions about the effectiveness of conventional  portfolio diversification," said Ricky Siao, a hedge fund specialist at Swiss private bank UBP.The investment environment has become more challenging for investors who have historically relied on traditional allocations to equities and fixed income, he added.As a result, investors are increasingly seeking exposure to strategies such as arbitrage, event-driven investing and quantitative macro strategies to reduce their dependence on equity market returns.Lowering the barriersThe democratization of hedge fund investing is taking shape through a growing array of investment vehicles, often with lower fees, smaller minimum investments and more frequent opportunities to withdraw money.Some of the biggest names in the hedge fund industry are already moving in that direction.Billionaire investor Bill Ackman's Pershing Square raised $5 billion in April for a publicly listed closed-end fund, giving everyday investors access to its investment expertise without the performance fees traditionally associated with hedge funds. The fund charges a 2% annual management fee.British hedge fund giant Man Group, meanwhile, entered the U.S. ETF market last September and doubled its lineup to four actively managed funds just three months later.The broader shift is also changing how hedge fund strategies are packaged for individual investors."What has changed most is the wrapper, not the strategy itself," said Yi Ling Ong, managing partner and chief operating officer at Golden Horse Fund Management.watch nowIn other words, hedge fund strategies are increasingly being packaged in more accessible vehicles such as mutual funds and ETFs, often with lower investment minimums and fewer restrictions on withdrawals."Investors may still be getting exposure to long/short equity, credit, or macro strategies, but delivered through vehicles that offer quarterly or monthly liquidity and standardized reporting."The trend is playing out across markets.In Europe, hedge fund managers have adapted strategies to fit regulated UCITS funds, which are accessible to individual investors. In the U.S., mutual funds and ETFs have similarly broadened access to alternative investment strategies.In Asia, digital wealth platforms are helping bridge the gap between institutional and individual investors.Singapore-based Endowus, which began offering hedge funds on its platform in 2022, has lowered minimum investments for semi-liquid funds to $50,000, while removing minimums altogether for some daily-liquid alternative funds, according to Chief Investment Officer Hugh Chung.While most hedge funds on the platform remain restricted to accredited investors, a growing number of alternative funds are becoming available to non-accredited investors, Chung said.India is seeing a similar shift through Specialized Investment Funds, or SIFs, which allow investors to access more sophisticated strategies through structures that more closely resemble traditional mutual funds, said Rajesh Singla of Alpha AMC.Assets under management in India's Specialized Investment Funds have more than quadrupled since March to 426.7 billion rupees as of end-October, according to data from the Association of Mutual Funds in India.The products carry a minimum investment of 1 million rupees, significantly below the entry thresholds typically associated with traditional hedge funds.The end of '2 and 20'?The shift is also making hedge fund-style investing cheaper.Traditional hedge funds have long been associated with the "2 and 20" fee model, which typically charges a 2% annual management fee and taking 20% of investment profits.While those fees have come under pressure over the years, retail-friendly alternatives such as hedge fund-like ETFs typically charge a single annual management fee of between 0.4% and 1.25%, according to Ong.The key risk is that investors may underestimate the complexity and risk associated with these strategies simply because they are now more accessible.Rajesh SinglaAlpha AMCBut lower fees does not necessarily mean better outcomes.Retail investment vehicles often face tighter regulatory and liquidity requirements, which can limit managers' ability to replicate strategies used by traditional hedge funds.Steinbrugge said those constraints can force managers to avoid less liquid securities that may offer some of the greatest opportunities for outsized returns."What investors are really choosing between is not just price, but structure," Ong said.The risks of going mainstreamThe industry's expansion into the retail market is also raising questions about whether individual investors fully understand the complexity of the strategies they are buying into.Easier access does not eliminate the risks associated with leverage, short selling or illiquid investments."The key risk is that investors may underestimate the complexity and risk associated with these strategies simply because they are now more accessible," Singla said.Liquidity is another concern, particularly for less liquid alternative investments being marketed through retail-friendly structures.Some interval funds, which are increasingly being used to distribute private credit and other alternative investments to individuals, may offer to repurchase only 5% of their outstanding shares each quarter, Steinbrugge said.That could leave investors unable to withdraw as much money as they want during periods of market stress.Still, industry watchers largely see the rise of retail-friendly products as complementary to traditional hedge funds rather than an existential threat to them.While the proliferation of more liquid, transparent and lower-fee products could intensify competition and pressure traditional fee structures, Siao does not expect retailization to fundamentally reshape the industry in the foreseeable future."I would expect this to be an incremental evolution rather than a fundamental transformation of the hedge fund business model," he said."Over time, the industry will likely remain segmented," Ong said. "Retail vehicles will address accessibility and scale, while hedge funds will continue to focus on depth, flexibility, and outcomes that are difficult to replicate in simplified formats."

schema.headline: Hedge funds are no longer just for the rich. They’re wooing everyday investors

title: Beware higher correlation but nab high U.S. credit yields, fund managers say
description: POLAND - 2025/02/24: In this photo illustration, an Artificial Intelligence (AI) logo is displayed on a smartphone with an Artificial Intelligence (AI
body: POLAND - 2025/02/24: In this photo illustration, an Artificial Intelligence (AI) logo is displayed on a smartphone with an Artificial Intelligence (AI) symbols on the background. (Photo Illustration by Omar Marques/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesThe artificial intelligence boom could lead to a recession, whether through a collapse in AI investment or widespread job losses as the technology advances, a hedge fund manager said."I do worry that if we don't have an AI-led recession in a few years, we're going to have an unemployment-led recession," Sheru Chowdhry, founder and chief investment officer at DSC Meridian Capital, said during a panel discussion moderated by CNBC's Joanna Ossinger at the iConnections Global Alts Asia conference in Singapore last week.Chowdhry's warning highlights a risk that extends beyond a potential bursting of the AI bubble. Rapid advances in the technology could lead to widespread job losses, with implications for the housing market and consumer spending, he said."If this continues to go at the pace it is, I think in a few years a lot of us will probably not have jobs," Chowdhry said, adding that investors would have to rethink their approach to sectors such as housing and discretionary spending.Even so, the fund manager remains bullish on computing power and sees opportunities in data centers, despite concerns about AI valuations.Beyond the AI hypeThe current AI investment cycle reminds Chowdhry of the dot-com bubble and the telecommunications infrastructure buildout of the early 2000s."This cycle reminds me of the dot-com bubble and the telecom build we had going on in the early 2000s," he said. "Every cycle is different, but it kind of rhymes in some ways."Chowdhry also questioned whether semiconductor companies could sustain their profit margins in the coming years.However, he sees opportunities in data centers, pointing to access to power and grid connections as major bottlenecks in the AI buildout."If you can identify data centers, I feel like that's going to be the picks and shovels of this cycle," he said.In particular, data centers that can secure permits and access to power within the next two years present a significant investment opportunity, he added.Beyond AI infrastructure, Chowdhry also pointed to attractive yields in U.S. credit markets.He cited yields of around 8.5% on U.S. high-yield bonds and 9.5% on leveraged loans, describing the current market environment as an opportunity to "get paid to wait."Hidden portfolio risksInvestment portfolios may be more vulnerable to market volatility than they appear, according to Dan Gelernter, director of AI at R.G. Niederhoffer Capital Management, who spoke on the same panel.Average monthly correlations across investable assets rose from around 5% between the 1960s and 1990s to roughly 11% to 12% by 2020, according to research cited by Gelernter.His own analysis suggests that the figure has climbed further to around 15% to 16% in 2026."Most portfolios are more highly levered, less liquid, more highly correlated than they appear to be, and that problem will get worse the more markets move," Gelernter said.Within the AI trade, Joo Kian Ong, a partner at AP3X Capital, said Samsung Electronics would be a good long position, with SK Hynix or Micron on the other side as potential shorts.

schema.headline: Beware higher correlation but nab high U.S. credit yields, fund managers say

title: Ukraine tells Putin to ‘stop complaining’ over oil refinery attacks as Russia promises retaliation
description: In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin holds a Security Council meeting in Moscow
body: In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin holds a Security Council meeting in Moscow on November 6, 2026.Mikhail Metzel | Afp | Getty ImagesUkrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has told Russian President Vladimir Putin to "stop complaining" over attacks on Russian refineries, saying Putin could end Kyiv's strikes on the oil facilities by bringing an end to the Kremlin's nearly five-year-long war.His comments come shortly after Russia's president told a meeting of government officials and senior oil executives in the Kremlin on Tuesday that Ukraine continues to attack refining facilities despite U.S. President Donald Trump's appeal to refrain from doing so. "I would like to note that retaliatory action from our side is inevitable. Everyone must be aware of that," Putin said, according to Russian state news agency Tass. In September, Trump called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks were "hurting the world" as fuel supply disruptions from the wars in Ukraine and Iran propelled U.S. diesel prices to a record high. Moscow welcomed Trump's push for Ukraine to halt strikes on Russia's diesel-producing facilities at the time. "If Putin doesn't like Ukraine's strikes on his oil refineries, he can order an end to the war," Ukraine's Sybiha said Tuesday via social media."If he doesn't want his military vessels hit, he can order an end to the war. Not to mention the 432,000 Russian soldiers he has lost on the battlefield this year without coming any closer to the goals of his invasion. Clearly, he doesn't care about them. Stop complaining. End the war," he added. CNBC could not independently verify the figures.In July, the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that about 1.4 million Russian troops were killed, wounded or went missing between the start of the full-scale invasion in Feb. 2022 and June 2026, with more than 30,000 casualties a month in the first half of this year.Satellite view of thick black smoke rising from multiple fires at Rosneft's Novokuybyshevsk Oil Refinery in Samara Oblast, Russia, on October 30, 2026.Gallo Images | Gallo Images | Getty ImagesUkraine has stepped up attacks on Russian critical targets in recent weeks, damaging Putin's prized Crimea bridge, striking a Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea and destroying one of Russia's newest ships at a Libyan port.Kyiv has also targeted Russian energy infrastructure. Zelenskyy said earlier this month that Ukraine's long-range strikes had disabled more than 55% of Russia's oil-refining capacity, describing this as a "justified response to Russia's refusal to de-escalate and its strikes on our energy infrastructure."Putin: Fuel supply situation remains 'challenging'Ukrainian drones reportedly struck two major Russian oil refineries in Russia's Samara region overnight, triggering fires at both facilities. Satellite images published in late October also showed black smoke rising from multiple fires at Rosneft's Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in southern Russia following a suspected Ukrainian drone attack.   Putin on Tuesday said Russia's fuel market situation remains "challenging" and called on government officials and oil executives "to continue reacting promptly to the supply-demand relationship for fuel across the whole territory of Russia," according to Interfax.Ukraine's allies have warned the country faces another winter of blackouts and freezing temperatures amid escalating Russian energy strikes.

schema.headline: Ukraine tells Putin to ‘stop complaining’ over oil refinery attacks as Russia promises retaliation

title: North Korea's Kim calls for nuclear arsenal expansion, says status 'will never change'
description: This picture taken on February 15, 2026 and released by North Korea's official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on February 16, 2026 shows North Kore
body: This picture taken on February 15, 2026 and released by North Korea's official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on February 16, 2026 shows North Korean leader Kim Jong Un delivering a speech at the inauguration ceremony of Saeppyol Street in Pyongyang. (Photo by KCNA VIA KNS / AFP via Getty Images) / South Korea OUTStr | Afp | Getty ImagesNorth Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for bolstering the country's nuclear arsenal and expanding the use of tactical nuclear weapons across multiple domains, state media reported Thursday, as Pyongyang reaffirmed its determination to retain its nuclear arms.Kim's comments followed a working visit Wednesday to facilities involved in nuclear material production and weapons research, according to the Korean Central News Agency.At the Nuclear Weapons Institute, he urged greater attention to "operationalizing" tactical nuclear weapons for a range of missions.Kim directly linked the development of those weapons to North Korea "sharing a border with its most dangerous, hostile state," an apparent reference to South Korea.The visit was part of Pyongyang's efforts to counter what Kim described as "the reckless expansion of adversary states' nuclear forces and military alliances," according to KCNA. He also singled out South Korea as a threat to North Korea's security and sovereignty.Kim reiterated that North Korea's status as a nuclear-armed state was irreversible, dismissing "denuclearization rhetoric" and saying its nuclear status "will never change.""[Our nuclear policy] is a core element of safeguarding the sovereignty of the Republic, enshrined in the supreme law of the state," he added.The report did not identify the sites Kim visited or disclose any production figures.The announcement followed an assessment last week by the International Atomic Energy Agency that another extension to Yongbyon's original uranium-enrichment facility had been externally completed by late October.The nuclear watchdog has lacked access to North Korea since 2009 and monitors its activities using satellite imagery and open-source intelligence.Citing what he portrayed as growing threats from Washington and its allies, Kim accused the U.S. of encouraging neighboring allies to acquire nuclear-powered submarines, pursuing nuclear sharing and the joint use of nuclear weapons.His comments come after South Korea announced efforts to acquire nuclear-powered submarines after President Donald Trump backed the plan in October 2025, according to a White House joint fact sheet. Nuclear-powered propulsion does not itself mean that a vessel carries nuclear weapons.Trump had expressed interest in meeting with Kim at the APEC summit in Shenzhen last week, according to Reuters, but no meeting took place and North Korea did not publicly respond to the proposal.U.S. President Donald Trump meets with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un at the demilitarized zone separating the two Koreas, in Panmunjom, South Korea, June 30, 2019.Kevin Lamarque | ReutersTrump denied that Kim had ignored him, adding that communications could "start up right away," in an interview with the New York Post Tuesday. He said the two leaders had not been in contact "recently.""We've been off to other things," Trump added.North Korea has continued to accelerate its nuclear weapons development and rebuff South Korean and U.S. attempts to resume dialogue since negotiations between Trump and Kim collapsed in 2019.— CNBC's Jenny Lee contributed to this report.

schema.headline: North Korea's Kim calls for nuclear arsenal expansion, says status 'will never change'

title: Fed’s preferred inflation gauge accelerated to 3.8% in October, raising the 2027 stakes for the central bank
description: Inflation moved further away from the Federal Reserve's target in October, reinforcing expectations that another interest rate hike is in the cards fo
body: Inflation moved further away from the Federal Reserve's target in October, reinforcing expectations that another interest rate hike is in the cards for December and raising questions about how much more work the central bank will have to do in 2027.The personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, showed a seasonally adjusted 3.8% annual inflation rate, in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate and nearly twice the central bank's goal. The reading was 0.1 percentage point higher than September.Excluding food and energy, core PCE was 3.3%, the Commerce Department reported Wednesday. That was 0.1 percentage point above the forecast.While the Fed officially follows the headline figure, policymakers consider core to be a more reliable longer-term gauge of inflation trends.A separate report also showed much stronger economic growth for the third quarter, with gross domestic product rising at a 4.3% annualized rate, according to a revised Commerce Department estimate. The strong top-line gain for the economy adds further fuel to the notion that Fed monetary policy is not restricting economic activity.Consumer spending rose 0.3% for the month, which matched the pace of price increases but was 0.1 percentage point lower than forecast. Income, on the other hand, surged 0.7%, much more than the 0.4% estimate. The personal saving rate rose to 4.1%.Stock market futures added to losses following the release, while Treasury yields also were sharply lower. Even with the higher-than-expected core inflation figure, expectations eased a bit for Fed rate hikes in 2027. Traders continued to price in two more increases but lowered odds for a third hike to about 1-in-3, compared to 50-50 on Tuesday, according to the CME Group's FedWatch. "Inflation is too hot and it will not be brought under control as long as economic demand is also too hot," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds.The report comes with the market fully pricing in a quarter percentage point interest rate hike when the Fed meets Dec. 8-9. Less certain is how much more rates will need to increase to get inflation back down to the Fed's 2% target. Inflation has been running above target for some 5½ years.Inflation had been drifting lower but spiked again following the late-February attacks on Iran led by the U.S. and Israel. Tariffs also have continued to exert pressure, as has strong demand associated with the artificial intelligence buildout. The White House on Wednesday announced a fresh round of tariffs on 14 trading partners including China, the European Union and Japan.Policymakers generally consider factors such as tariffs and supply shocks to be temporary, but some fear the impact has begun spreading through the economy and could become embedded."America's inflation problem is bigger than an energy shock," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. The large upward increase in GDP came from revisions to investment as well as consumer and government spending. Consumer spending, which accounts for about two-thirds of all economic activity, rose 4.2% in the third quarter. A metric known as real final sales to private domestic purchasers, which Fed officials regard as a key indicator of underlying demand, jumped 5.8%, reflecting an upward revision of 0.9 percentage point.In other economic news Wednesday, the Labor Department reported that initial jobless claims slipped to 189,000 for the week ending Nov. 21, down 13,000 from the prior week and back to around the lowest level since the late 1960s. Wall Street had been expecting 200,000.

schema.headline: Fed’s preferred inflation gauge accelerated to 3.8% in October, raising the 2027 stakes for the central bank

title: How Trump’s latest tariff moves hand India an edge over rival Asian exporters
description: US President Donald Trump (R) prepares to shake hands with India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi during a bilateral meeting as part of the G7 summit, i
body: US President Donald Trump (R) prepares to shake hands with India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi during a bilateral meeting as part of the G7 summit, in Evian, eastern France, on June 17, 2026. Mandel Ngan | Afp | Getty ImagesThe latest U.S. tariff rates announced Wednesday have signaled that Washington is willing to offer India an edge over its competitors if New Delhi agrees to finalize a long-pending trade deal.The Office of the United States Trade Representative has proposed a tariff of 17% on Indian exports if New Delhi "were to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade" with Washington. It added that without a trade deal, India could face tariffs of up to 25% under Section 301 investigations encompassing excess production capacity that harms U.S. interests.Meanwhile, the USTR has proposed tariffs of 18% on Bangladesh, Cambodia, Thailand, and 20% on China and Vietnam, subject to their respective trade deals, handing India a competitive advantage over rival exporters.The U.S. expects the announcement of a lower tariff rate will encourage New Delhi to sign off on a trade deal before the G20, Atman Trivedi, partner at Washington-based DGA Albright Stonebridge Group, told CNBC. India has got a "better bargain with Washington than its main competitors," and it may be enough for the Indian government "to declare victory and secure domestic backing for the deal," Trivedi said.In February, U.S. President Donald Trump had announced a deal with India, claiming that New Delhi had accepted to "Buy American" at a much higher level after the U.S. agreed to slash tariffs to 18% from 50% earlier. U.S. pressureThe India-U.S. trade deal has been pending with both sides indicating there was little room to grant concessions, while the Supreme Court annulling Trump tariffs allowed New Delhi to demand preferential tariffs that give it an edge over competitors."Today's announcement increases the urgency of reaching an agreement," Ronak D. Desai, visiting fellow at Hoover Institution, Stanford University, told CNBC. He added that while the prospect of a 17% tariff may strengthen the economic case for the deal, the threat of a 25% tariff could stir the sensitivity of the Indian government."The Modi government will be particularly sensitive to any perception that India is conceding under American Pressure," Desai said.India's commerce ministry on Wednesday said it "does not have structural excess capacity in any sector," denying the findings of the USTR investigation, but added that it remains committed to "working closely with the United States towards the early conclusion of the India-U.S. Bilateral Trade Agreement."Despite India facing steep tariffs, which were raised to 50%, New Delhi's trade surplus with the U.S. rose to $57.3 billion in 2025 from $45.2 billion in 2024.Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Trump are likely to meet in December for the G20 leaders' meeting in Florida, and several experts believe the two leaders could seal the trade deal on the sidelines of the summit.

schema.headline: How Trump’s latest tariff moves hand India an edge over rival Asian exporters

title: Judge blocks FCC early-renewal process for Disney-owned ABC stations, for now
description: FILE PHOTO: The logo of the ABC television network is pictured during the ABC network presentation to the Television Critics Association in Pasadena,
body: FILE PHOTO: The logo of the ABC television network is pictured during the ABC network presentation to the Television Critics Association in Pasadena, California July 19, 2006. Fred Prouser | ReutersA judge has temporarily blocked the Federal Communications Commission from continuing its early renewal of a set of broadcast station licenses for Disney-owned ABC.Judge Loren L. AliKhan of U.S. District Court in Washington granted Disney the preliminary injunction it sought and denied the FCC's attempt to dismiss the suit."This is not a close case," wrote the federal judge. "Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face—loss of their broadcast licenses—the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness."The broadcast network had filed the lawsuit and followed the FCC beginning its early review of the ABC licenses. The government agency cited concerns around ABC's diversity, equity and inclusion efforts as the reason behind the start of the early renewal — years ahead of their scheduled expiration."Today's decision is an important victory for the First Amendment," said an ABC spokesperson.An FCC spokesperson said in a statement that the part of the decision granting ABC's motion "is wrong on the facts and wrong on the law," the Associated Press reported.In her ruling, AliKhan said that early license renewal proceedings came over a year into the FCC's enforcement push against ABC, starting with an investigation into Disney's employment practices in March 2025 and leading to the renewal proceedings in April this year.ABC on Tuesday had said that it continued to "face irreparable harm" from the administration, which "has been acting" through the FCC, which is run by President Donald Trump appointee Brendan Carr.AliKhan, a Joe Biden appointee, noted in her ruling that ABC had to change how it handled guest appearances for top shows "The View" and "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" with no candidate for public office appearing on the former and a senatorial candidate's appearance on the latter uploaded to YouTube instead of being broadcast."The prospect of license non-renewal has also factored into plaintiffs' calculus of when and how they cover President Trump and political topics," said the judge.ABC had alleged that Trump and Carr have been making comments "intended to chill their protected speech," and that such comments have escalated since the 2024 presidential election.The White House and the FCC didn't immediately respond to requests for comment from CNBC.— CNBC's Dan Mangan contributed to the story

schema.headline: Judge blocks FCC early-renewal process for Disney-owned ABC stations, for now

title: South Korea upgrades growth forecast, raises benchmark rates to highest in two years
description: The Bank of Korea (BOK) in Seoul on Dec. 28, 2024.Kim Jae-Hwan | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesSouth Korea's central bank on Thursday hiked benchmark lend
body: The Bank of Korea (BOK) in Seoul on Dec. 28, 2024.Kim Jae-Hwan | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesSouth Korea's central bank on Thursday hiked benchmark lending rates to their highest in two years, as inflation continues to run above target while a booming economy allows it room to tighten policy. The central bank raised rates by 25 basis points to 3.25% for its final meeting of the year, in line with expectations from economists, data on the Bank of Korea's website showed.Inflation is expected to remain above its 2% target level for a considerable time, the BOK added in its statement, saying this was due to the pass-through of elevated cost pressures and as demand-side pressures also gradually strengthen, driven by stronger economic growth. Inflation in the country stood at 2.8% in October.The BOK also upgraded its growth forecasts for 2026 to 3.9% for 2026 and 4.1% for 2027, up from the 3.3% and 2.9%, respectively, forecast in August.South Korea's third-quarter GDP grew by 3.4% year on year, beating expectations, allowing the central bank room to raise rates. "The projections of high growth rates for next year and beyond also reflect the significantly increasing weight of the IT sector as a growth engine for the Korean economy," BOK Governor Shin Hyun-song said at a press conference following the decision. Operating profits in the semiconductor sector could reach 700 trillion won, Shin told reporters, according to local news agency Yonhap. Shin also signaled that more rate hikes, although he did not give a fixed timeline.  "While the domestic economy is expected to continue its robust growth, inflation is forecast to remain above the target level for a considerable time ... The Board, therefore, sees it warranted to continue its policy response until there is confidence that inflation will converge stably to the target level."Gareth Leather, senior Asia Economist at Capital Economics said there is reason to believe that the BOK's tightening cycle was drawing to a close. The BOK has raised rates by 75 basis points in five months, as higher energy prices from the Iran war and the AI boom has pushed up inflation in the country. Leather said that the country's strong growth, as well as a strengthening won could ease concerns over inflation.While rapidly rising property prices could strengthen the case for a prolonged tightening cycle, Leather said that the BOK was "more likely to favour macroprudential measures over further rate hikes to address its financial stability concerns."After the decision, the country's benchmark Kospi rose 1.88%.

schema.headline: South Korea upgrades growth forecast, raises benchmark rates to highest in two years

title: Macy's postpones Thanksgiving Day Parade due to severe weather
description: Workers inflate the Joe Cool and Woodstock balloon during Macy's Balloon Inflation 2026 in New York City, Nov. 25, 2026.Adam Gray | Getty ImagesMacy's
body: Workers inflate the Joe Cool and Woodstock balloon during Macy's Balloon Inflation 2026 in New York City, Nov. 25, 2026.Adam Gray | Getty ImagesMacy's on Wednesday announced it's postponing its Thanksgiving Day Parade, originally scheduled for Thursday, due to severe weather.The parade, held each year on Thanksgiving morning, will now take place on Saturday at 8:30 a.m. ET, according to the company. The New York City area is expected to have heavy rain and thunderstorms on Thanksgiving."The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our city and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," Macy's said in a statement.This year's event marks the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. The annual event has never been canceled due to weather, though it was suspended between 1942 and 1944 for World War II.The parade's viability this year had been in question after concerns arose over strong winds that could become dangerous for the massive balloons that the event is known for. Many of the balloons had already been inflated as of Wednesday afternoon. The postponement also means thousands of volunteers and artists slated to perform will have to adapt to Saturday's schedule.

schema.headline: Macy's postpones Thanksgiving Day Parade due to severe weather

title: Saudi national in OpenAI bugging case is out on bond after DOJ tries to block release
description: Photo of Abdulrahman Alfozan checking a recording device in OpenAI's office in San Francisco, according to the Department of Justice.Courtesy: U.S. De
body: Photo of Abdulrahman Alfozan checking a recording device in OpenAI's office in San Francisco, according to the Department of Justice.Courtesy: U.S. Department of JusticeAbdulrahman Alfozan, the Saudi national accused of bugging an executive conference room at OpenAI's headquarters, has been released from custody, his attorney told CNBC on Wednesday.The confirmation of Alfozan's release came a day after a federal judge in San Francisco said the defendant would be allowed out of jail on a $1 million bond, despite prosecutors' warnings that he posed a serious flight risk.Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer, is expected to be fitted with an ankle monitor, his attorney, David Rizk, previously told CNBC.Alfozan was scheduled to be released from detention Wednesday morning at 8 a.m. PT. Shortly before that deadline, U.S. Attorney Craig Missakian of the Northern District of California urged the court to maintain Alfozan's detention pending trial, "given the significant risk that the defendant will flee to Saudi Arabia if he is released from custody."In an order posted on the case docket later Wednesday, Judge Vince Chhabria said the court only learned of the government's last-minute bid to block Alfozan's release after he had already been let out.The government's motion "is therefore denied as moot," Chhabria's order stated. The judge set a hearing for Dec. 3 on the bid to revoke the magistrate judge's order releasing Alfozan.Pointing to Alfozan's "ample resources, significant family and professional ties to Saudi Arabia, and few remaining ties to the United States," Missakian had argued in a court filing that the release conditions imposed by Magistrate Judge Alex Tse "are insufficient to safeguard the defendant's appearance for future proceedings in this case."Alfozan "presents a serious risk of flight that no set of release conditions can reasonably mitigate," Missakian wrote.His office sought to pause the magistrate judge's release order until a ruling on a motion to revoke it. The Department of Justice did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Alfozan's release.Tse in a court hearing Tuesday ruled in favor of Rizk's motion for his client's release, which said prosecutors have admitted finding "no new evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia."In a text message to CNBC after that hearing, Rizk said, "We are simply grateful that the Court made the right decision to release Mr. Alfozan and now we look forward to defending the case."But Missakian's filing Wednesday morning pushed back, saying "the government's investigation of this seven-week-old case is ongoing."Prosecutors have so far found "hundreds of audio files" on Alfozan's personal computer, "including dozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that occurred at OpenAI throughout September 2026, at least one of which involved representatives of a foreign government and many of which involved discussions of what may be trade secrets," according to the filing."To be sure, what the defendant did or intended to do with those audio files remains under investigation, but the absence of that evidence at this point has no bearing" on whether Alfozan is a flight risk, Missakian argued.Alfozan was arrested Oct. 9 and is accused of concealing a recording device in the artificial intelligence company's conference room to secretly record discussions. The device was found in a USB port in a television in the room on Sept. 30, prosecutors have said.Jury selection for Alfozan's trial is scheduled to begin Jan. 20.— CNBC's Dan Mangan contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Saudi national in OpenAI bugging case is out on bond after DOJ tries to block release

title: ‘Ready for any storm’: UAE minister optimistic on economy as IMF lifts forecast
description: Minister of Economy and Tourism, Abdulla Bin Touq Al Marri, speaks during a press briefing held by the UAE government following Iranian strikes, in Ab
body: Minister of Economy and Tourism, Abdulla Bin Touq Al Marri, speaks during a press briefing held by the UAE government following Iranian strikes, in Abu Dhabi on March 3, 2026. Iran stepped up its attacks on economic targets and US missions across the Middle East on March 3, as the US president warned it was "too late" for the Islamic republic to seek talks to escape the war. As drones and missiles crashed into oil facilities and US embassies in the Gulf, Washington's ally Israel bombarded targets in Iran and pushed troops deeper into Lebanon to battle the Tehran-backed militia Hezbollah. (Photo by Ryan Lim / AFP via Getty Images)Ryan Lim | Afp | Getty ImagesThe UAE is "very optimistic" about achieving 7%-8% growth next year, the country's economy and tourism minister Abdulla bin Touq Al Marri told CNBC after the latest data from the International Monetary Fund showed the country would avoid a recession in 2026.The IMF last week revised the UAE's real GDP forecast to 0.2% growth in 2026 from a 3.9% contraction predicted a month ago. "The UAE is coming back, and that adjustment within one month shows that there is a huge potential aspect when it comes towards the end of the year," the minister told CNBC's Dan Murphy.He said the tourism industry was already picking up with occupancy rates returning to "almost near normal" and international carriers including British Airways and Air France rerouting flights to the UAE. The minister expects economic growth to be higher than 0.2% this year. The Iran war has disrupted economic activity in the UAE, with missile and drone attacks from Tehran and maritime disruptions weighing on energy trade, tourism, aviation and private-sector confidence.Earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump said that renewed attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" if negotiations produce a "very strong agreement." However, on Monday, Trump threatened that Tehran could face fresh U.S. strikes next year if the two countries failed to strike a deal, as per Fox News.   "We can we cannot promise the world for any storms that will land on our shore, but we can always promise that the UAE's economy is ready for any storm," Al Marri said. He added that next year the UAE's economy will have a "different" model than the one before the conflict and investments will be focused on building factories and "things that we really need in times of crisis."The World Bank in October said it expects the UAE's economy to recover next year, driven by rising oil production and exports and a rebound in tourism, trade, transportation, financial services, and construction. It warned that the improvement in economic activity in the UAE largely depends on the duration and intensity of the Iran war, with a faster de-escalation likely to accelerate the recovery in services exports and private-sector activity.

schema.headline: ‘Ready for any storm’: UAE minister optimistic on economy as IMF lifts forecast

title: Norse Atlantic flights suspended after warning finances 'critical'
description: A Norse Atlantic Airways Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner prepares for takeoff at Los Angeles International Airport at the start of the Labor Day holiday on Au
body: A Norse Atlantic Airways Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner prepares for takeoff at Los Angeles International Airport at the start of the Labor Day holiday on August 31, 2023 in Los Angeles, California.Aaronp/bauer-griffin | Gc Images | Getty ImagesSome Norse Atlantic flights were cancelled on Wednesday and Thursday, raising concerns about the future of the low-cost long-haul airline shortly after it warned that it was in a "critical financial situation."Shares of Norse closed 53.3% lower on Wednesday after plunging as much as 86% during the session.The airline had been set to operate two Pakistan International Airlines flights Wednesday under a wet-lease agreement, in which one airline provides the aircraft and crew to another. The agreement had only been signed in early October.But PK786 from London to Islamabad and PK710 from Manchester to Lahore were cancelled because of "an unexpected operational suspension," the Pakistani flag carrier said on X.Norse Atlantic has yet to make an official statement on its operational status. Checks by CNBC showed the airline was still selling tickets as at 1:30 a.m. Oslo time on Thursday.PIA said it would operate the routes using its own Boeing 777 aircraft from Wednesday.Norse's own flight Z0 783 from London Gatwick to Orlando was also shown as canceled Wednesday on live air traffic website Flightradar24. London Gatwick's website listed the flight's status for Thursday as "enquire airline."In a bid to stave off financial troubles, Norse cut 75 jobs in May as part of an effort to reduce costs by $50 million, after Eivind Roald replaced founder Bjorn Tore Larsen as CEO in November last year.The Norwegian carrier said Wednesday that its situation depended on securing financing for short-term liquidity needs and that it was in discussions about a potential strategic takeover."Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution," the airline said.India's largest airline, low-cost carrier IndiGo, entered an agreement with Norse Atlantic in early 2025 to lease six 787-9 aircraft as it launched flights to Europe and Britain ahead of the arrival of its own widebody planes.The agreement concluded at the end of October this year, with IndiGo citing airspace constraints, elevated fuel costs and currency pressures.At its peak in 2024, Norse Atlantic had 4,822 scheduled flights. That number dipped to 4,695 in 2025 and 2,565 in 2026, according to aviation analyst Cirium. The airline had 122 flights scheduled for November this year.Norse Atlantic CEO Roald told CNBC in May that he was not "overly concerned" about access to fuel and said the airline had no indication at the time that the crisis would have an immediate impact. The airline said in October that it was continuing to operate at reduced capacity because of "prolonged high fuel prices."watch now

schema.headline: Norse Atlantic flights suspended after warning finances 'critical'
